title: KV cache amplification triage notes
summary: Notes and preliminary runbook for a recurring overnight incident where KV cache miss amplification in a subset of dedicated GPU workers caused cascading latency and eventual pool degradation. Focused on detection, fast mitigation steps, and long-term guardrails.
content:
Problem statement:

Over the 2025-10-29 -> 2025-11-01 midnight windows we observed repeated latency spikes and increased token cost for customers on a subset of dedicated GPU pools. Root effect: sustained tail latency increase in the serving runtime from 30ms median to 600ms p95 for generation calls. Investigation suggests a KV cache amplification pattern: worker nodes repeatedly warming large per-request KV prefix entries which evicted useful cache items and caused excessive memory pressure and CPU GC activity on those nodes.

Why this is different from a normal noisy neighbor: the behavior is non-CPU-bound fine-tuning style jobs that trigger wide, sparse KV writes (tokenization-heavy prefixes) which look like cache storms rather than single-job saturation. This caused transient OOMs in the serving process and flapped autoscaler decisions.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 2025-10-29 23:45: first alert: pool-a latency p95 crossed 300ms (alert: pool.latency.p95 > 250ms for 2m)
- 2025-10-30 00:03: error budget decrement; autoscaler launched 4 extra nodes, but several nodes reported "OOM in allocator" and were drained by SRE operator
- 2025-10-30 00:10: oncall checked dashboards, noticed sudden increase in KV cache churn metric (kv.cache.evictions/sec) and increase in per-process RSS growth
- 2025-10-30 00:28: temporary mitigation applied: reduce max-concurrent-requests per worker to 1 on affected machines (patch via rollout), which reduced tail but did not fully restore pool health
- 2025-11-01 01:15: second recurrence after a partial rollback change from a scheduled deploy that increased batch-size for some models

Signals collected:
- Metrics: kv.cache.hits, kv.cache.misses, kv.cache.evictions, process.rss_bytes, process.heap_gc_ms, gpu.utilization, gpu.memory.total_used
- Alerts fired: pool.latency.p95, pool.evictions.rate, node.process.oom_count
- Logs: repeated patterns of "kv: write-prefix size=XXKB" from serving-runtime at trace level on affected nodes

Quick commands and checks (paste-able):
- kubectl -n dedicated get pods -l pool=pool-a -o wide
- kubectl -n dedicated logs <pod> -c serving-runtime --since=10m | grep -E "kv: write-prefix|evicting key" -n
- curl -s http://prometheus.internal/api/v1/query?query=kv_cache_evictions_per_sec | jq .data
- ssh node (<node>) && sudo pmap -x $(pgrep serving-runtime) | head -n 20

Hypotheses (ordered by confidence):
1) Client workloads doing many short, unique prompts cause sparse KV writes leading to cache thrash. The new batch-size tweak in the last deploy encouraged workers to surface more unique prefixes per request.
2) A regression in eviction policy where a newly-introduced scoring factor gives short-lived prefixes lower retention priority, so once storm happens, eviction amplifies. (linked PR: /pull/812).
3) Under-provisioned GPU memory combined with driver-level fragmentation leads to per-process memory growth triggering allocator OOM.

Immediate mitigations applied and rationale:
- Throttle concurrency on the pool (max-concurrent-requests -> 1) for affected nodes to reduce simultaneous warmups. Rationale: reduces simultaneous unique writes and gives cache time to stabilize.
- Pin fallback routing: route heavy KV workloads to burst-backend tier with larger cache size (manual routing rule for affected customers). Rationale: isolate to nodes with larger cache configuration.
- Reverted the batch-size increase for the flagged model (rollout-id: rdo-2025-10-30-42). Rationale: reproduce step and prevent further amplification.

Post-incident root cause analysis (preliminary):
- The combination of a config change (batch-size bump) + eviction scoring change in serving-runtime created a conjunctive failure mode: more unique prefixes per second + faster eviction of slightly older entries -> cache misses proliferated -> memory allocations for KV entries spiked -> GC pressure + allocator fragmentation -> per-process RSS rose -> OOMs and process restarts -> autoscaler misinterpreted restarts as capacity shortage, leading to churn.

Detection rules to add (draft):
- New alert: kv.cache.eviction_amplification_score > 500 for 5m (score is a weighted function: evictions/sec * new_prefix_rate).
- Add p99 tracking for kv.cache.warmup_latency and alert if > 200ms for 3m.
- Alert if node.process.oom_count > 1 in 10m and kv.cache.evictions/sec > 50.

Runbook draft: Immediate steps for oncall
1) On receiving pool.latency.p95 alert, go to pool dashboard and check kv cache charts (hits/misses/evictions). If evictions spike and new_prefix_rate > 100/s, proceed to step 2.
2) Identify top offending workloads: run internal query to list models by kv.write_rate: curl .../query?model=*&sort=write_rate_desc (replace with actual endpoint). If a single customer/model at top, contact SE/CS to ask for a temp throttle.
3) Apply emergency throttle: kubectl patch cm pool-config-pool-a -p '{"data":{"max_concurrent_requests":"1"}}' && rollout restart daemonset/pool-a-serving-runtime
4) If processes show OOM in logs, cordon node and drain gracefully: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
5) If autoscaler is oscillating due to churn, temporarily set min_replicas to current count and pause autoscale decisions: POST to autoscale-api /pause with reason "kv-cache-amplification incident"
6) Post-mitigation: gather heap profiles and kv key distribution dump: curl http://<pod>:8080/debug/kv/distribution > /tmp/kv-distro.json and attach to JIRA-INFRA-2347.

Longer-term mitigations / engineering work items (backlog):
- Change eviction policy to penalize thrash patterns (RFC in confluence). Owner: Marcus Lee. Target: Q1 2026.
- Introduce per-customer kv write rate limits at the router layer to prevent single tenant blast radius. Owner: Elena Gómez. Target: Q4 2025 (MVP).
- Add fragmentation-aware allocator or periodic compaction in the serving-runtime to reduce RSS growth over time. Owner: Serving runtime team (see PR 812).
- Autoscaler guard: add hysteresis when node restarts coincide with high kv eviction rates to avoid scaling loops. Owner: SRE infra.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are there clients intentionally doing many unique short prompts (e.g., embedding generation with unique prefixes) or is this a buggy client? Need CS to check usage patterns for top offending model IDs.
- Does GPU driver fragmentation contribute significantly or is the issue solely at the serving-runtime heap? Need allocations profile under load with nvprof.

Action items assigned (short):
- Ava: synthesize a deterministic load test that reproduces amplification locally using a workload generator (due 2025-11-07).
- Ravi: instrument kv cache with per-prefix TTL and a thrash score metric (due 2025-11-21).
- Elena: implement emergency per-customer write-rate limiter at the edge (MVP due 2025-12-15).
- Marcus: write eviction-policy RFC and schedule design review (due 2025-11-14).

Appendix: useful logs (sanitized)
[2025-10-30T00:01:12Z] serving-runtime INFO pid=2341 kv: write-prefix key="user-123:prompt-xyz" size=16384 time_ms=12
[2025-10-30T00:01:12Z] serving-runtime WARN pid=2341 kv: evicting key="model-cache:abc" reason="score_low"
[2025-10-30T00:01:14Z] kernel ERROR cgroup: memory cgroup out of memory: kill process 2341 (serving-runtime)

Notes to next oncall:
- If you triage this, check whether a deploy happened in the previous 30 minutes (git ops deploys list). If yes, roll back immediately and follow runbook.
- Keep CS looped when throttles or routing changes affect customer latency. We prefer temporary routing over node drains when customers are sensitive to latency.

Draft runbook checklist (copyable):
- [ ] Confirm alert and open JIRA-INFRA-2347
- [ ] Check kv cache metrics and identify top offending model IDs
- [ ] Apply emergency throttle if single-customer traffic is responsible
- [ ] If multiple customers causing pool-wide amplification, pause autoscaler and route to burst-backend
- [ ] Collect kv distribution and heap profiles before restarting processes
- [ ] Sanitize artifacts and attach to ticket

Proposed dashboard tiles to add (short names):
- KV cache: evictions/sec (pool, node)
- KV new_prefix_rate (pool, model)
- KV thrash_score (derived)
- node.process.rss_bytes by process (p95/p99)
- autoscaler.scaling_events (count, reason)

End of notes. Will convert into a cleaner runbook page once the RFC and first engineering fixes land.

Last edit notes: 2025-11-10 09:12 UTC by Ava Martinez — added detection rules and assigned owners.
